PBS Utah Donor Prediction — Exploratory Data Analysis¶

IS 6813 MSBA Capstone · Fall 2026 · Kate Klinger

1. Introduction¶

Business problem¶

PBS Utah depends on tens of thousands of individual donors, most of whom give small monthly or annual gifts. Gift officers can only personally cultivate a limited number of donors each year (each officer portfolio has room for 125). PBS Utah needs a way to identify which donors are likely to give — and to give more — next fiscal year, so that renewal, upgrade, and cultivation efforts go where they produce the most revenue.

Analytic problem¶

Using donor history through fiscal year t, predict each donor's giving in fiscal year t + 1. The unit of analysis is the donor-year. Candidate targets:

  • Amount given in FY t + 1 (regression; heavily right-skewed),
  • Retention: whether the donor gives at all in FY t + 1 (classification),
  • Upgrade: whether FY t + 1 giving exceeds FY t giving, or crosses the $1,000 major-donor threshold.

Because officers can contact only a limited number of donors, the model will ultimately be used to rank donors, so ranking quality (e.g., lift in the top decile) matters more than exact dollar accuracy.

Questions guiding this EDA¶

  1. How are the tables related, and do the keys join cleanly?
  2. What data quality problems (missing, constant, duplicated, or placeholder values) must be handled?
  3. What does the target look like — how skewed is giving, how many donors renew, upgrade, or lapse each year?
  4. Which parts of a donor's history (recency, frequency, amount, recurring vs. one-time, tenure) are associated with next-year giving?
  5. Which constituent attributes are usable, and which are snapshot fields that would leak the future?
  6. Are solicitation volume and Passport viewing associated with giving?
  7. What does the cultivation program's design (staggered rollout with random holdouts) let us learn about the effect of officer contact?

2. Setup and data loading¶

The data come from the course repository. Several tables are stored with Git LFS, so clone the repository and run git lfs pull (a GitHub ZIP download gives tiny pointer files instead of data). Point DATA_DIR at the tables/ folder. The CSVs are not committed to this repository.

All rows are synthetic; no row is a real person or gift.

In [1]:
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.ticker as mtick
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns

DATA_DIR = Path("../data/tables")  # folder holding the course CSVs

pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 50)
pd.set_option("display.width", 160)
pd.set_option("display.float_format", "{:,.2f}".format)
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", context="notebook")
plt.rcParams["figure.dpi"] = 110
BLUE, ORANGE, GREY = "#2a6fdb", "#e8833a", "#9aa0a6"


def to_fy(dates):
    # PBS Utah fiscal years run July-June; FY2026 = July 2025 - June 2026
    dates = pd.to_datetime(dates)
    return dates.dt.year + (dates.dt.month >= 7).astype(int)

soft = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "soft_credits.csv", parse_dates=["Credit Date"])

Join findings.

  • Every documented key is unique except soft_credits."Credit ID": 79 rows are exact duplicates (a known issue in the dictionary). They must be dropped before summing.
  • Every foreign key finds its match except SYN-ORPHAN, which appears on 2% of payment rows (33,733 payments) and on 79 soft credits. These gifts belong to no constituent, so they count toward revenue but cannot be attributed to a donor.
  • Legacy rows link to constituents through constituent_id_1/_2 only (_3–_7 are always blank). 18% of legacy rows link to nobody.
  • Designation Detail ID is not a usable join key between soft credits and payments. Two designation values ("Designation 1" and "Other") cover about 880,000 payments, so a merge on that column explodes into a many-to-many join.

def missing_summary(df, name):
    out = df.isna().mean().rename("share missing").to_frame()
    out["table"] = name
    return out[out["share missing"] > 0]

Constant and placeholder columns¶

Because the data are synthetic, many columns hold a single placeholder value (e.g., "Synthetic"). These carry no information and should be dropped before modeling.

Data-quality findings and how I will handle them.

Issue Handling
59 constant or blank columns. In the legacy table only gift_kind, gift_type, gift_date, payment_amount, state, zip, and the ID columns carry information. In campaign_codes only Communication Method varies. UofU degree and employment fields are blank throughout, as the dictionary warns. Drop them.
Organization payments mirror soft credits. SYN-ORG-DAF/SYN-ORG-SOFT hard-credit payments almost exactly match deduplicated soft credits each year (e.g., FY2026: $448K vs. $452K). They are the same money. Count it once, as the person's giving via the soft credit. Exclude org rows from donor-level giving.
1,086 payments of $0. Drop (the definition uses positive payments).
Major Donor Class is 99.7% blank. Marital Status only ever says "Married" (91% blank). Treat blank as "not recorded", not as a category like "single".
Address City is a placeholder. 26% blank. Use state / ZIP instead.
tender_type = "Legacy" is on 43% of Unite payments but is not in the reference dictionary. Note it; it may be a synthetic artifact. Don't rely on tender type without asking.
rollout_fy blank for one portfolio (P08). Blank means the portfolio never adopted the program. It is not missing data.

5. Building the target: donor fiscal-year giving¶

Following the Student Data Dictionary convention, a donor's fiscal-year giving is

the sum of positive payments the constituent made, plus positive soft credits assigned to the constituent, after exact duplicate rows are removed.

Organization payments (SYN-ORG-*) are excluded from person-level giving because the same gifts reach people through soft credits; counting both would double count. SYN-ORPHAN payments are excluded because they belong to no constituent.

In [9]:
person_pay = pay[(pay["payment_amount"] > 0) & ~pay["donor_id"].isin(org_ids + ["SYN-ORPHAN"])]
person_soft = soft.drop_duplicates()
person_soft = person_soft[(person_soft["Credit Amount"] > 0) & (person_soft["Soft Credit Constituent ID"] != "SYN-ORPHAN")]

giving = (
    pd.concat(
        [
            person_pay[["donor_id", "fy", "payment_amount"]].rename(columns={"payment_amount": "amount"}),
            person_soft.rename(columns={"Soft Credit Constituent ID": "donor_id", "Credit Amount": "amount"})[["donor_id", "fy", "amount"]],
        ]
    )
    .groupby(["donor_id", "fy"], as_index=False)["amount"].sum()
)

# wide donor x FY matrix, 0 = no giving that year
wide = giving.pivot(index="donor_id", columns="fy", values="amount").fillna(0)
print(f"{len(giving):,} donor-years from {giving['donor_id'].nunique():,} donors")
wide.head()

Payment revenue held steady at $3.0–3.4M a year** from FY2021 to FY2025, then **jumped 27% to $4.27M in FY2026. Organization hard credits add 7–10% each year, and orphan payments add about 2%. The FY2026 jump matters for validation: if FY2026 is the test year, the model will be scored on a year that looks different from the years it learned from.

# concentration: what share of revenue comes from the top x% of donors?

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.plot(pct * 100, cum * 100, color=BLUE)
ax.plot([0, 100], [0, 100], color=GREY, ls="--", lw=1)
ax.set(title="Concentration of FY2025 giving", xlabel="Top % of donors", ylabel="% of giving")
plt.tight_layout()
{f"top {p}%": f"{cum.iloc[int(len(s) * p / 100) - 1]:.0%} of giving" for p in [1, 5, 10, 20]}
Out[12]:
{'top 1%': '12% of giving',
 'top 5%': '22% of giving',
 'top 10%': '34% of giving',
 'top 20%': '54% of giving'}

The target is extremely right-skewed and lumpy.

  • The median donor gives **$60 a year**: a $5-a-month sustainer. The 90th percentile is $240 and the 99th is $600, but the maximum is $73,360.
  • Amounts cluster at multiples of 12 ($60, $120, $240), because most donors give monthly.
  • Giving is concentrated but not extremely so: the top 1% of donors give 12% of the money, the top 10% give 34%, and the top 20% give 54%.
  • Only 83–130 donors a year (about 0.3%) give $1,000 or more. A "major donor" classifier would face severe class imbalance.

Modeling implication: Raw dollars are a poor regression target. Better options are log(amount), or a two-part model: P(give next year) × E(amount | gives).

Retention, upgrades, and new donors¶

In [13]:
rows = []
for y in wide.columns[1:]:
    prev, cur = wide[y - 1] > 0, wide[y] > 0
    both = prev & cur
    rows.append({
        "fy": y,
        "donors": cur.sum(),
        "retained from prior FY": both.sum(),
        "new or reactivated": (cur & ~prev).sum(),
        "lapsed": (prev & ~cur).sum(),
        "retention rate": both.sum() / prev.sum(),
        "upgrade rate (of retained)": (both & (wide[y] > wide[y - 1])).sum() / both.sum(),
        "downgrade rate (of retained)": (both & (wide[y] < wide[y - 1])).sum() / both.sum(),
    })
flow = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("fy")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
flow[["retained from prior FY", "new or reactivated"]].plot.bar(stacked=True, ax=ax, color=[BLUE, ORANGE], rot=0)

In [14]:
# where do donors move between giving bands from one year to the next?
bands = [-np.inf, 0, 50, 100, 250, 1000, np.inf]
labels = ["$0", "$1-50", "$51-100", "$101-250", "$251-999", "$1,000+"]
trans = pd.DataFrame({
    "from": pd.cut(wide[2025], bands, labels=labels),
    "to": pd.cut(wide[2026], bands, labels=labels),
})
trans = trans[trans["from"] != "$0"]
mat = pd.crosstab(trans["from"], trans["to"], normalize="index")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
sns.heatmap(mat, annot=True, fmt=".0%", cmap="Blues", cbar=False, ax=ax)
ax.set(title="FY2025 band -> FY2026 band (row %)", xlabel="FY2026 giving", ylabel="FY2025 giving")
plt.tight_layout()

Donors are quite stable.

  • Year-over-year retention runs 75–80%. Among retained donors, roughly a fifth upgrade and a fifth downgrade.
  • Each year adds 7,000–8,700 new or reactivated donors and loses a similar number. FY2026 is the exception: 12,124 new donors and an upgrade rate of 26.5%.
  • The transition matrix shows strong persistence. 77–80% of donors in the $51–100 and $101–250 bands (the sustainer bands) stay in the same band.
  • The **$1–50 band is mostly one-time donors and half of them lapse**. The two highest bands are the most volatile: only 47% of $1,000+ donors stay at $1,000+, and 10% of the $251–999 band moves up to $1,000+.

7. Giving history as predictors¶

To look at predictors the way a model will see them, I build a donor-year panel: one row per donor who gave in FY t, with features computed only from information available through FY t, and outcomes from FY t + 1. FY2021–FY2025 serve as feature years (FY2026 has no following year in the data).

Pre-FY2021 history comes from the legacy table. Legacy rows can list several household members; for features (has this person given before? since when?) each linked person gets credit, but those rows are never summed into revenue.

In [15]:
# legacy history per constituent (credit every household member listed; used for tenure, not revenue)
id_cols = [f"constituent_id_{i}" for i in range(1, 8)]
leg_long = legacy.melt(id_vars=["fy"], value_vars=id_cols, value_name="donor_id").dropna(subset=["donor_id"])
leg_hist = leg_long.groupby("donor_id")["fy"].agg(legacy_first_fy="min", legacy_last_fy="max", legacy_years="nunique")

first_fy = pd.concat([leg_hist["legacy_first_fy"], giving.groupby("donor_id")["fy"].min()]).groupby(level=0).min()

# payment-type mix per donor-year
mix = person_pay.assign(recurring=person_pay["pledge_gift_type"].eq("Recurring")).groupby(["donor_id", "fy"]).agg(
    n_payments=("payment_amount", "size"),
    any_recurring=("recurring", "max"),
    max_gift=("payment_amount", "max"),
)

panel = []
for t in range(2021, 2026):
    d = pd.DataFrame(index=wide.index[wide[t] > 0])
    d["fy"] = t
    d["amount_t"] = wide.loc[d.index, t]
    d["amount_t_minus_1"] = wide.loc[d.index, t - 1] if (t - 1) in wide.columns else np.nan
    recent = [c for c in wide.columns if t - 2 <= c <= t]
    d["years_gave_last3"] = (wide.loc[d.index, recent] > 0).sum(axis=1)
    d["tenure_years"] = t - first_fy.reindex(d.index)
    d["amount_next"] = wide.loc[d.index, t + 1]
    panel.append(d.reset_index())
panel = pd.concat(panel, ignore_index=True)
panel = panel.merge(mix.reset_index(), on=["donor_id", "fy"], how="left")
panel["any_recurring"] = panel["any_recurring"].fillna(False).astype(bool)  # soft-credit-only years have no payment rows
panel["retained"] = panel["amount_next"] > 0
panel["upgraded"] = panel["amount_next"] > panel["amount_t"]
panel["log_amount_t"] = np.log10(panel["amount_t"])
panel["log_amount_next"] = np.log10(panel["amount_next"].where(panel["amount_next"] > 0))
print(f"Panel: {len(panel):,} donor-years, {panel['donor_id'].nunique():,} donors")
panel[["amount_t", "amount_next", "years_gave_last3", "tenure_years", "n_payments", "retained", "upgraded"]].describe()

In [17]:
def rate_plot(ax, col, data=None, order=None, title=None):
    data = panel if data is None else data
    r = data.groupby(col, observed=True).agg(retention=("retained", "mean"), n=("retained", "size"))
    if order is not None:
        r = r.reindex(order)
    ax.bar(r.index.astype(str), r["retention"], color=BLUE)
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.PercentFormatter(1))
    ax.set(ylim=(0, 1), title=title or col, ylabel="Gave next FY")
    for i, (v, n) in enumerate(zip(r["retention"], r["n"])):
        ax.text(i, v + 0.02, f"{v:.0%}\nn={n:,}", ha="center", fontsize=8)
    return r

panel["giving_band"] = pd.cut(panel["amount_t"], bands[1:], labels=labels[1:])
panel["tenure_band"] = pd.cut(panel["tenure_years"], [-1, 0, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50], labels=["new", "1-2", "3-5", "6-10", "11-20", "21+"])
panel["donor_type"] = np.where(panel["any_recurring"], "Recurring (sustainer)", "One-time only")

donor_type giving_band        
One-time only $1-50 45,102 50.8% 26.9% $5
$51-100 6,855 50.2% 4.9% $5
$101-250 3,038 58.0% 9.1% $7
$251-999 948 69.1% 13.5% $250
$1,000+ 332 81.6% 9.9% $600
Recurring (sustainer) $51-100 60,463 92.1% 15.3% $60

$251-999 1,649 92.6% 8.7% $250
$1,000+ 172 95.9% 8.7% $600

Giving history is the strongest signal, and recurring status dominates.

  • This year's giving predicts next year's well: Spearman ρ = 0.65 for all donors, and r = 0.69 on the log scale for retained donors.
  • Recurring (sustainer) donors retain at about 92% no matter how much they give, how long they have given, or how many recent years they gave. One-time donors retain at only about 50%. Their retention climbs with gift size ($251–999 → 69%, $1,000+ → 82%) and is lowest for brand-new donors (43%).
  • Measured on all donors, recency/frequency (years given in the last three: 73% → 82%) and tenure (new 73% → 1–2 years 79%) look like modest predictors. Most of that pattern comes from recurring donors being concentrated in the longer-tenure groups. Within each donor type, the effect is small.
  • Upgrades come mostly from small one-time donors: 27% of the $1–50 group upgrade, many of them by starting a recurring gift. The $251+ one-time givers are the likeliest pool for moving up to $1,000+.
  • The recurring share of donors rose from 59% (FY2021) to 69% (FY2025). That shift alone pushes retention up over time.

Modeling implication: Build features for recurring status, gift size, gift count, and recency/frequency, and include their interactions with donor type. Tree-based models will capture those interactions without extra work.

8. Constituent attributes and leakage¶

The constituents table describes each person as of the end of the data (FY2026). Some fields are stable (gender, state). Others, such as the sustainer flag, major-donor class, annual giving group, and age, are snapshots that would leak future information if used as features for earlier years.

In [19]:
people = con[con["Primary Constituent Type"] != "Organization"].copy()
people["ever_gave"] = people["Constituent ID"].isin(wide.index)
for col in ["Annual Giving Group", "Sustainer PBS Utah", "Major Donor Class PBS Utah", "Marital Status"]:
    people[col] = people[col].fillna("(blank)")
leak = {col: pd.crosstab(people[col], people["ever_gave"], margins=True) for col in ["Sustainer PBS Utah", "Annual Giving Group", "Major Donor Class PBS Utah"]}
pd.concat(leak, names=["field", "value"]).rename(columns={False: "never gave", True: "gave FY21-26", "All": "total"})

These snapshot fields leak the outcome.

  • Every current sustainer gave in FY2021–26. That is true by definition.
  • Every Annual Giving Group other than ND, and every Broadcaster or Director, gave.

These fields record the donor's status at the end of the data. Using them to predict FY2025 → FY2026 giving would be using FY2026 information to predict FY2026. Recurring status should instead be rebuilt from payments in each feature year (any_recurring above). Age is also a snapshot, but it can safely be rolled back (Age − (2026 − t)).

Constituent attributes add almost nothing. Retention is about 78% in every group: every age band, every gender, Utah vs. elsewhere, and with or without a spouse record. Median giving is $60 everywhere, and the recurring share is about 65% in every age group. Mean giving rises only slightly with age ($90 → $101).

The University of Utah giving fields are the exception. Lifetime UofU Fundraising correlates with total PBS giving (Spearman 0.56). These are also snapshot values with no date, so whether they can be used depends on when they were recorded. That question should go to Jeff / PBS.

Modeling implication: Keep a few stable demographics as candidates, but expect little lift from them. This synthetic data seems to put nearly all of its signal into giving behavior.

Solicitations are frequent, but on their own they say little about who will give.

  • About 0.5–1.1 million solicitations go out each year, roughly 11 per person solicited. Same-code response rates are low and falling, from 2.1% in FY2021 to about 1.3%.
  • Response rates are similar for the legacy, miscellaneous, digital, and mail codes (1.2–1.5%). They are lower for email, phone, and in-person codes (0.3–0.9%). Those personal channels are probably used on harder-to-reach groups, so the lower rates are not evidence that the channels perform worse.
  • Once donor type is accounted for, the number of solicitations is not related to retention. Solicited one-time donors retain at about 52% and sustainers at about 92%, however often they were solicited. (The odd "0 solicitations" group of one-time donors has only 13 donor-years.)

Modeling implication: Solicitation count is mostly a byproduct of donor status. Who gets solicited is decided by PBS, so this table cannot show whether solicitation causes giving. It is a weak candidate feature.

Passport viewing shows no association with retention in this data. Retention is 78–79% at every viewing level, and the median gift is $60 for viewers and non-viewers alike. Drama, History, and Science & Nature are the most-watched genres. Passport is a member benefit, so viewing mostly reflects that someone is already a donor. It does not help predict which donors will give more.

Caveat: A year with no viewing rows can mean no account, no consent, or no viewing, so "no viewing" is a mixed group.

11. The cultivation program¶

Each year from FY2022 to FY2025, eight officer portfolios each selected 125 donors (1,000 per year). Within each portfolio, about a quarter of the selected donors were randomly held out from contact. Portfolios adopted the cultivation program in a staggered rollout (FY2023–FY2026, one never). This design is valuable: the random holdout lets us estimate the causal effect of contact, and the staggered rollout lets us compare contact before and after a portfolio adopted the program.

def amt(donor, year):
    return wide.at[donor, year] if (donor in wide.index and year in wide.columns) else 0.0

c = cult.copy()
c["giving_prior"] = [amt(d, y - 1) for d, y in zip(c["synthetic_id"], c["fiscal_year"])]
c["giving_same"] = [amt(d, y) for d, y in zip(c["synthetic_id"], c["fiscal_year"])]
c["giving_next"] = [amt(d, y + 1) for d, y in zip(c["synthetic_id"], c["fiscal_year"])]
c["change_next_vs_prior"] = c["giving_next"] - c["giving_prior"]
# a handful of five-figure gifts swamp the means, so also cap each year's giving at $2,000 (~99th percentile)
CAP = 2000
c["change_capped"] = c["giving_next"].clip(upper=CAP) - c["giving_prior"].clip(upper=CAP)
c["gave_next"] = c["giving_next"] > 0
c["upgraded"] = c["giving_next"] > c["giving_prior"]
c["has_soft_credit"] = c["synthetic_id"].isin(person_soft["Soft Credit Constituent ID"])
c["group"] = np.where(c["contacted"], "Contacted", "Holdout")
c["program"] = np.where(c["program_adopted"], "After adoption", "Before adoption")

# who gets selected? compare with all donors that year

    "selected donors": c.groupby("fiscal_year")["giving_prior"].median(),
    "all donors": giving.assign(fiscal_year=giving["fy"] + 1).groupby("fiscal_year")["amount"].median(),
}).loc[2022:2025]

Cultivation findings.

  • Selection is not random. Officers pick donors whose median prior-year giving is $120, twice the typical donor's $60. A third of selected donors have a soft credit (DAF or sponsor gift), against 4% of all donors. A selected-vs.-unselected comparison would therefore be biased, but the random holdout makes contacted vs. holdout a fair comparison.
  • Raw dollar means are dominated by a few five-figure gifts: one holdout donor's giving went from $2,000 to $39,212. Capping each year's giving at $2,000 gives a much clearer picture.
  • Before a portfolio adopts the program, contacted and held-out donors look alike: +$12 (SE $14), with identical upgrade rates.
  • After adoption, contacted donors' giving rises by about **$68 more** than holdouts' (SE $19), and their upgrade rate is 7 points higher (36% vs. 28%). The difference-in-differences is about +$55 (SE $24).

Business implication: The program appears to work, so the question shifts from "who will give the most?" to "for whom does contact make the biggest difference?" That is an uplift-modeling question. The data have 992 holdout donor-years in total, about 124 per portfolio. That is enough to explore differences in the effect, but only coarsely.

12. Results¶

Summary of findings¶

  1. Data structure. The nine tables join cleanly on constituent ID. The exceptions are SYN-ORPHAN gifts (2% of payments), 79 duplicated soft credits, and unlinked legacy rows (18%). 59 columns are constant or blank and can be dropped.
  2. Building the target. Fiscal-year giving = positive personal payments + deduplicated soft credits, with org hard credits excluded to avoid double counting. This yields 199,772 donor-years for 71,811 donors, FY2021–26.
  3. Target shape. Giving is highly skewed: median $60, 99th percentile $600, maximum $73K. Only about 0.3% of donors reach $1,000 a year. Retention is 75–80%. FY2026 is an unusual year: revenue +27% and 12K new donors.
  4. Strongest predictor. Recurring status (sustainers retain at 92% vs. 50% for one-time donors), followed by gift size and recent giving.
  5. Weak or no signal. Demographics, solicitation volume, and Passport viewing show almost no association once donor type is accounted for.
  6. Leakage. Snapshot fields (sustainer flag, giving group, major-donor class, age) must not be used as-is for past years. Rebuild them from dated transactions, or roll them back.
  7. Cultivation works after adoption. Contact raised capped giving by about $68 relative to random holdouts, a 7-point higher upgrade rate. Before adoption there was no effect.

Implications for modeling¶

  • Unit and target. Use donor-year rows with features from FY ≤ t and outcomes from FY t+1. Use a two-part target (retain × amount), or log amount. Evaluate on ranking metrics, such as revenue captured in the top 125 per portfolio.
  • Validation. Split by time (train on FY2021–24 → FY2025 outcomes, test on FY2025 → FY2026) or by household, never randomly by row. Expect a shift in FY2026.
  • Features to build. Recurring flag, last-year amount, max gift, payment count, years given in the last 3, tenure (including legacy history), soft-credit/DAF flag, and age at t.
  • Next step. Because cultivation has a measurable effect, consider an uplift model (e.g., a two-model or T-learner on contacted vs. holdout) so that officers pick the donors whose giving changes most when contacted, not just the biggest givers.

Open questions for the sponsor¶

  • What does tender_type = "Legacy" mean in Unite payments?
  • What explains the FY2026 jump in revenue and new donors: a campaign, or a data artifact?
  • When were the UofU giving fields captured? Can they be used for earlier years?
  • What exactly does "contacted" mean in portfolios that had not yet adopted the program?
